stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Beat writers' outlook, from Jack Kerouac's On the Road (1957) and Allen Ginsberg's Howl (1956). The Beats rejected the suburban lifestyle, the consumer society, and cold war patriotism. They prized spontaneity, freedom, and artistic improvisation, and they praised jazz, travel, and Eastern spirituality.

stem: The Beat movement of the 1950s most directly prepared the way for which development of the 1960s?

options.text: The counterculture of hippies who rejected middle-class values
The election of a president who promised a New Frontier
options.misconception: Background from the books: Kennedy's election came from politics, not from Beat writing.

options.text: The passage of laws ending segregation in public places
options.misconception: Background from the books: civil rights laws came from the movement and Congress, not from Beat writing.

options.text: The growth of suburbs around every large American city
options.misconception: The Beats rejected the suburbs, so they did not prepare the way for suburban growth.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Beats' rejection of suburbs, buying, and patriotism became the hippies' rejection of middle-class values a decade later.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Kennedy's election came from politics, not from Beat writing.
rationales.C: Background from the books: civil rights laws came from the movement and Congress, not from Beat writing.
rationales.D: The Beats rejected the suburbs, so they did not prepare the way for suburban growth.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: the Beats were few, but their books traveled widely among the young.
2. Background from the books: the Beats prepared the way for the hippies, who took the same rejection further.
3. Background from the books: the same values, spontaneity, freedom, and distrust of middle-class life, reappear in the 1960s counterculture.
Remember: A small literary rebellion can set the style for a much larger youth movement.
